clue.text: Insects foremost in carrying disease (8)

indicators.note: the foremost part of a word is the bit at the front, its first letter

blocks.note: first letter of carrying
a bone disease caused by lack of vitamin D

explanation.surface: A warning that certain insects lead the way in spreading illness.
explanation.walkthrough: "Foremost in carrying" reads like insects leading the way in spreading illness; it only wants the C.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain category definition: the answer names one family of chirping insects.

clue.text: Family husky, not a thoroughbred of course (9)

indicators.note: literally says the word goes without an A

blocks.note: race = family line, stock
HOARSE (husky, of a voice) without its A

explanation.surface: Someone insists the family's husky dog is no pedigree animal, of course.
explanation.walkthrough: "Husky" looks like the sled dog but is the voice sense, HOARSE. "Of course" is not a throwaway: it places the thoroughbred on a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: a thoroughbred that runs on a racecourse, with 'of course' punning on the stock phrase.

clue.text: Drink, maybe Coke, put out with name removed (5)

indicators.note: N is the abbreviation for name, and removed says take it away

blocks.note: coke is a fuel; a burnt-out piece of it is a cinder

explanation.surface: A drink, perhaps a Coke, gets served without its brand name.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital-C Coke suggests the fizzy drink, but it is the fuel: a piece of coke that has gone out is a cinder.
explanation.definitionFit: A category definition: the answer is one kind of drink, fermented from apples.

clue.text: Basil’s worked with these institutes (11)

indicators.note: letters that are worked are kneaded like dough into a new shape

blocks.note: anagram fodder; the apostrophe is ignored
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Basil has done his work with these institutions.
explanation.walkthrough: "Institutes" reads as a plural noun beside "these", but it is the verb: to institute is to set up.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, both verbs in the third person: to institute a practice is to set it up.

clue.text: Wearing small garment, provided it’s taken up (3,4)

indicators.note: whoever is wearing a garment is inside it, so IF goes inside KILT

blocks.note: S (small) + KILT, the Scottish pleated skirt
provided = if; goes inside KIL|T

explanation.surface: Wear the short garment, as long as it has been shortened.
explanation.walkthrough: "Taken up" sounds like a hem being raised; the definition means the thing people ride up the mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: skiers take it up the slope, the hem sense of 'taken up' being the decoy.

clue.text: Gets out puzzles (6)

blocks.note: cricket: the wicketkeeper breaks the wicket while the batsman is out of his ground
a verb here: baffles

explanation.surface: Someone finds a way out of puzzles.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket: a wicketkeeper stumps a batsman by breaking the wicket while he is out of his ground, which gets him out.
explanation.definitionFit: Two verb senses: a cricketing dismissal, and the everyday sense of baffling someone.

clue.text: The odds of deals being turned down (3)

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters: first, third, fifth
something turned round faces the other way, so read it backwards

blocks.note: letters 1, 3, 5 of DEALS

explanation.surface: A card player hears that the chances of being dealt a good hand have been refused.
explanation.walkthrough: "Odds" and "deals" sound like betting and cards, and "turned down" like a refusal; "down" is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: feeling down means unhappy.

clue.text: Football team eating fruit, almost without restraint (9)

indicators.note: a team eating fruit takes it inside
almost the whole word: all but its last letter

blocks.note: as in Manchester United, Leeds United
LIME without its last letter; goes inside UN|ITED

explanation.surface: A football side stuffs itself with fruit, almost without holding back.
explanation.walkthrough: UNITED is the stock football team in British crosswords, from the many clubs with that name.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: with no limits means without restraint.

clue.text: A little gift is opened up in advance (5)

indicators.note: only a little of the phrase is used, a run of letters inside it
in a down clue, up means read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the letters run across giFT IS OPened

explanation.surface: A small present is unwrapped before the day.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a child opening a present early; "in advance" is not timing but the definition, advance as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to advance an idea is to put it forward as true.

clue.text: Like some tea and cakes? (4)

blocks.note: tea served cold, over ice, rather than hot
cakes with a hard sugar coating on top

explanation.surface: An afternoon tea spread.
explanation.walkthrough: One word does two jobs: iced tea is served cold, while an iced cake is covered in sugar icing.
explanation.definitionFit: One adjective in two senses, chilled for the tea and sugar-coated for the cakes.

clue.text: Child stars travelling economy (5,5)

indicators.note: letters that are travelling are on the move, out of their places

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: Young celebrities flying in the cheap seats.
explanation.walkthrough: "Travelling economy" reads as one phrase about flying; "travelling" is the instruction and "economy" alone the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym from travel: the cheapest class of ticket, once called by its number.

clue.text: Angel cake wrapper finally swallowed by fish (6)

indicators.note: what comes finally in each word is its last letter
what a fish swallows ends up inside it

blocks.note: a freshwater fish
last letters of cakE and wrappeR; go inside CH|UB

explanation.surface: A fish gulps down the wrapper from an angel cake.
explanation.walkthrough: "Angel cake" reads as one thing, a light sponge; the definition stops at "Angel".
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the answer is one order of angel, often drawn as a winged child.

clue.text: Secret signal (8)

blocks.note: adjective: private, personal
verb: to hint, to make known indirectly

explanation.surface: A covert sign.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are pronounced differently: IN-ti-mut (private) and IN-ti-mate (to hint).
explanation.definitionFit: Two words spelt alike: an adjective meaning private and a verb meaning to hint.

clue.text: Article about Rome uncovered by a country pamphleteer (6,5)

indicators.note: about means around, so the article goes around what follows
a word uncovered has its outer letters, its covers, stripped off
by means beside, so the country sits next to the A

blocks.note: the definite article; goes around the rest
ROME without its first and last letters
as printed
OM + A + SPAIN go inside TH|E

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece about Rome is exposed by some rural pamphlet writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Paine wrote the pamphlet Common Sense (1776), urging American independence.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Paine is the best-known writer of political pamphlets in English.

clue.text: Meat for hosts to cut is different (10)

indicators.note: a host holds guests inside, so PRO holds the rearranged letters
letters made different are put in a new order

blocks.note: pro = in favour of; takes the rest inside PR|O
anagram of TOCUTIS

explanation.surface: Hosts at a dinner find that carving this meat is a different matter.
explanation.walkthrough: "Meat for hosts" looks like a phrase about entertaining; "for" is PRO and "hosts" is the container instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the answer is an Italian cured ham, one kind of meat.

clue.text: Sportsman with a glove, pants and cap (9)

blocks.note: short trousers
to cap = to top, beat

explanation.surface: A player kitted out with glove, shorts and cap.
explanation.walkthrough: The shortstop is a baseball fielder positioned between second and third base; the glove, pants and cap all belong to his kit.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: a baseball fielder, who wears a mitt.

clue.text: Did jam start off as Bunter’s favourite? (4)

indicators.note: with its start taken off, the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: a drawer that jammed stuck

explanation.surface: Was jam the first thing Bunter loved?
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is the greedy schoolboy of British comic stories; tuck is school slang for sweets and snacks, his obsession.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by allusion: British school slang for snacks, which the greedy Billy Bunter craved.

clue.text: Sectarian rambling of a philosopher (9)

indicators.note: rambling letters wander off from their order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A philosopher's bigoted, meandering speech.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the adjective from Descartes, the French philosopher.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective defined by its source: it means relating to René Descartes.

clue.text: Check old rule out (4)

blocks.note: to vet = to check
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Look over an obsolete regulation.
explanation.walkthrough: "Old rule" reads as one noun phrase; "rule out" is the definition, a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to forbid by authority is to rule something out.

clue.text: House a witty new Democrat enters, sure of success (4,3,3)

indicators.note: what enters goes inside, so N and D go into the phrase A DRY

blocks.note: house = home
as printed
standard abbreviation
standard abbreviation; N and D go between A and DRY
dry wit is deadpan humour

explanation.surface: A clever new Democrat takes his seat in the House, confident of winning.
explanation.walkthrough: "House" and "Democrat" suggest Congress; the House is just HOME.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone safely home and dry has already succeeded.

clue.text: Text written about a pet dog (7)

indicators.note: about means around, so MS is written around the A

blocks.note: MS = manuscript; goes around A
as printed
a pet is a fit of sulking, a tiff

explanation.surface: A message written about someone's pet dog.
explanation.walkthrough: "Pet dog" reads as one phrase; "pet" is the old word for a sulk or petty quarrel, TIFF.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the answer is one large breed of dog.

clue.text: Bigheads putting in time for themselves? (8)

indicators.note: putting something in a word inserts it

blocks.note: egoists act for themselves; takes T inside EGO|ISTS
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Conceited people spending time only on themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that "for themselves" is a playful definition of EGOISTS, people out for themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang synonym: a bighead is a conceited person who talks up himself.

clue.text: Ghost town in Yorkshire by the sound of it (5)

indicators.note: what is said matches the answer's sound

blocks.note: Goole is a port town in East Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A deserted place in Yorkshire, or so it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: "Ghost town" reads as a single phrase; the definition is only "Ghost". Goole is a small port town in Yorkshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: an evil spirit, near enough to a ghost.

clue.text: Lead-free inspection on power supply (6)

indicators.note: free of its lead, the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
SURVEY without its first letter

explanation.surface: An inspection of the electricity supply checks it is free of lead.
explanation.walkthrough: "Lead-free" sounds like petrol or paint; here it removes the leading S. "On" places the rest after P.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal synonym for the verb, used of goods and provisions.

clue.text: Frantic turnover of local papers (5)

indicators.note: a turnover flips something over, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: your local is your nearby pub, a bar
identity papers

explanation.surface: A newspaper business in a frantic change of ownership.
explanation.walkthrough: "Local papers" suggests newspapers; a local is British slang for the neighbourhood pub, and papers are identity documents.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, the figurative sense of a disease that makes animals wild.

clue.text: Pasta mostly effective in hoop shapes (10)

indicators.note: most of the word: all but its last letter
in places the shortened word inside the shapes

blocks.note: plural of torus, a ring shape
TELLING (effective) without its G; goes inside TOR|I

explanation.surface: Most pasta works well in ring shapes.
explanation.walkthrough: These really are ring-shaped pasta, so the hoop shapes fit the scene. A torus is a doughnut shape; the plural is tori.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: small filled rings of Italian pasta.

clue.text: Non-professional set (3)

blocks.note: adjective: not of the clergy or a profession
verb: to put down, as a table is set

explanation.surface: An amateur group.
explanation.walkthrough: "Set" looks like a noun, a group; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: an adjective for non-experts, as in a lay reader, and a verb meaning to put down.

clue.text: Prematurely withdraw a bond (4)

blocks.note: informal verb: quit or jump out early
money pledged to secure a prisoner's release

explanation.surface: Cashing in a bond before it matures.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is finance, but the second sense is the courtroom: the security that frees someone awaiting trial.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: slang for pulling out early, and the legal pledge for release.

clue.text: Watery spot surrounding dock (6)

indicators.note: one word surrounding another wraps round it, so SPY is split to hold LOP

blocks.note: to spot = to spy; goes around LOP
to dock a tail is to lop it

explanation.surface: A marshy patch by the harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: "Spot" and "dock" both look like nouns, a place and a harbour; both are verbs.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, used of runny food or wet ground.

clue.text: Work by The Third Man novelist (8)

blocks.note: third man is a cricket position behind the batsman on the off side
Henry, 18th-century author of Tom Jones

explanation.surface: A book by the author of The Third Man.
explanation.walkthrough: The Third Man suggests Graham Greene's story, but third man is a cricket position, and the work done there is catching and stopping the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the cricket job of the player at third man, and the surname of an English novelist.
